lessons.name: Encapsulation — bundling data + methods, access modifiers
lessons.desc: Encapsulation binds data and methods that operate on that data together, restricting direct access to internal state. Access modifiers (private, protected, public) enforce boundaries.
lessons.q: Why does encapsulation protect object invariants and reduce coupling? How do access modifiers enforce boundaries?
lessons.qsub: Protects invariants, reduces coupling, makes refactoring safer. In interviews, demonstrate that you keep fields private and expose behavior, not data.
terms: Object ka apna internal data ya variables
Object ke methods ya functions jo us state ke saath kaam karte hain
private, public, protected jaise keywords jo ye decide karte hain ki kaun data dekh/change kar sakta hai
lessons.what:
Encapsulation ka seedha sa matlab hai data (variables) aur behavior (methods) ko ek hi dabbe (class) mein band karna, aur us dabbe ko bahar se direct modify karne se rokna.

Ye ek protective shield ki tarah kaam karta hai taaki koi bhi anjaan code aapke data ko directly na chhed sake.
lessons.analogy:
Socho ek medicine capsule ki tarah. Asli dawai (data) capsule ke andar safe rehti hai. Tum direct dawai (chemicals) se touch nahi hote, bas pura capsule khaa lete ho.

Ya phir ek ATM ka socho. Tum ATM ki tijori (private data) se direct cash nahi nikal sakte. Tumhe ATM ke buttons (public methods) use karke, sahi PIN daalna padta hai tabhi paise nikalte hain.
lessons.why:
Bina encapsulation ke, koi bhi external code tumhare object ka state change kar dega (jaise bank balance negative mein set kar dena).

Data ko chupa kar (private banakar) aur sirf methods ke through usko change allow karke, tum rules aur validation enforce kar sakte ho.

lessons.name: Inheritance — IS-A relationships, super/sub classes, method overriding
lessons.desc: Inheritance creates an IS-A hierarchy where a subclass inherits fields and methods from a parent class. Method overriding allows subclasses to provide specialized behavior.
lessons.q: Why does inheritance create tight coupling and when should you prefer composition over inheritance?
lessons.qsub: Promotes code reuse and establishes polymorphic relationships. But misuse leads to fragile hierarchies — prefer composition over inheritance.
terms: Wo class jiski khoobiyan inherit ki jaa rahi hain
Wo nayi class jo parent ki khoobiyan le rahi hai
Ye relationship batata hai ki child actually parent ka hi ek type hai (e.g. Car IS-A Vehicle)
lessons.what:
Inheritance ka matlab hai ek nayi class banana jo ek existing class ki properties (state) aur methods (behavior) ko automatically le leti hai.

Ye "IS-A" (yah-ek) relationship establish karta hai.
lessons.analogy: Biological inheritance ko socho. Ek bacha apne parents se aankhon ka rang (property) aur chalne ka tareeqa (behavior) inherit karta hai. Par bacha kuch apna naya talent bhi seekh sakta hai (e.g. coding karna) aur chalne ka tareeqa badal bhi sakta hai (Method Overriding).
lessons.why: Code duplication (DRY) se bachne ke liye. Agar tumhare paas Dog, Cat, aur Cow classes hain, toh sabme eat() aur sleep() likhne ke bajaay ek Animal class bana do aur sabko usse inherit kara do.

lessons.name: Polymorphism — compile-time (overloading) vs runtime (overriding)
lessons.desc: Polymorphism means "many forms". Compile-time polymorphism (method overloading) vs runtime polymorphism (method overriding, virtual dispatch).
lessons.q: How does polymorphism enable treating objects of different types uniformly through a common interface?
lessons.qsub: Enables treating objects of different types uniformly through a common interface. The foundation of Strategy, Command, and many behavioral patterns.
terms: Ek hi class mein same naam ke multiple methods, par parameters alag (Compile-time)
Child class apne parent ke method ko replace kar deti hai (Run-time)
lessons.what: Polymorphism ka seedha sa matlab hai "Bohot saare roop". Ek hi function ya method alag-alag objects ke liye alag tarike se behave kar sakta hai.
lessons.analogy: Socho ek TV ka remote hai, uspe "Power" button (method) hai. Agar tum TV ka remote use karoge toh TV on hoga, AC ka remote use karoge toh AC on hoga. Button (interface) same hai, par device (object) ke hisaab se kaam alag ho raha hai.
lessons.why: Kyunki humein if-else ke lambe chaude pahad nahi likhne hain. Agar sab objects ek common interface share karte hain, toh hum unhe uniform tarike se treat kar sakte hain.

lessons.name: Abstraction — abstract classes vs interfaces, hiding complexity
lessons.desc: Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential features. Achieved via abstract classes (partial impl + abstract methods) and interfaces (pure contracts).
lessons.q: How does abstraction reduce complexity for the caller and isolate change? What is the difference between abstract classes and interfaces?
lessons.qsub: Reduces complexity for the caller, isolates change, and enforces contracts. The "what" is separated from the "how".
terms: Aadhi-adhuri class jiska object (instance) nahi banaya jaa sakta
Sirf ek contract (rules) jisme koi implementation nahi hoti
lessons.what: Abstraction ka matlab hai zaroori details dikhana aur baaki ki complexity (background ka mess) chhupa lena.
lessons.analogy: Socho tum car chala rahe ho. Tumhe pata hai ki steering ghumane se car mudti hai aur break marne se rukti hai. Tumhe engine ke andar cylinders kaise kaam kar rahe hain, ye janne ki zaroorat nahi hai. Steering wheel ek "Abstraction" hai.
lessons.why: Kyunki system bohot complex ho jate hain. Caller (jo code use kar raha hai) ko bas yahi pata hona chahiye ki "kya" karna hai, "kaise" ho raha hai usse usko matlab nahi hona chahiye.

lessons.name: Association, Aggregation, Composition — has-a vs owns-a differences
lessons.desc: Association (uses-a), Aggregation (has-a, independent lifecycle), Composition (owns-a, dependent lifecycle). These define relationships with different ownership semantics.
lessons.q: What is the difference between association, aggregation, and composition? How does ownership affect lifecycle management?
lessons.qsub: Understanding relationship strength determines object lifecycle management. Composition implies destruction responsibility; aggregation does not.
lessons.what: Ye teeno HAS-A relationships ke alag alag levels (strength) hain.
lessons.analogy:
Association: Ek Doctor aur Patient (Dono azaad hain, bas ek doosre ko jante hain).
Aggregation: Ek College aur uske Teachers (Teacher College ka part hain, par College band hone ke baad bhi Teacher zinda rehta hai).
Composition: Ek Insaan aur uska Dil (Dil Insaan ka part hai, Insaan mara toh Dil bhi gaya).
lessons.why: Kyunki humein objects ke lifecycle ko manage karna hota hai. Agar do objects strongly coupled hain, toh ek ko delete karne par dusra bhi garbage collect hona chahiye.

lessons.name: SRP — Single Responsibility: one class, one reason to change
lessons.desc: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. Every class should be responsible for a single part of the system functionality.
lessons.q: Why do SRP classes lead to more cohesive, focused, and testable code? What is the God Object anti-pattern?
lessons.qsub: SRP leads to more cohesive, focused, and testable classes. Classes with multiple responsibilities are harder to change, test, and understand.
terms: Class ke change hone ki wajah (Reason to change)
Wo dheet class jo system ka aada kaam khud akele karti hai
lessons.what:
Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) kehta hai ki ek class ke paas badalne (change hone) ki bas ek hi wajah honi chahiye.

Matlab ek class ko system ka sirf ek hi kaam sambhalna chahiye.
lessons.analogy:
Socho ek restaurant ka scene. Waha ek Chef hai (khana pakata hai), ek Waiter hai (order leta hai) aur ek Cashier hai (bill banata hai).

Agar Chef ko hi khana pakana pade, bill bhi katna pade, aur table bhi saaf karni pade (God Object), toh busy time mein pura restaurant doob jayega. Har ek bande ki ek Single Responsibility honi chahiye.
lessons.why:
Jab ek class bohot saare alag alag kaam karti hai, toh unme aapas mein coupling ho jati hai. Agar tum email bhejne ka logic update karoge, toh galti se database save karne wala logic tut sakta hai.

SRP code ko chhota, cohesive aur test karne mein aasan banata hai.

lessons.name: OCP — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification
lessons.desc: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behavior through new code, not by changing existing code.
lessons.q: How does the Strategy pattern exemplify the Open/Closed Principle? Why prevents modifying tested code?
lessons.qsub: Prevents introducing bugs in working code. Achieved through polymorphism, inheritance, and composition. The Strategy pattern is a canonical example.
terms: Nayi features aasani se add ho sakein
Purana tested code na chhedna pade
lessons.what: Open/Closed Principle (OCP) kehta hai ki code aisa hona chahiye jismein nayi functionality add karna aasan ho (Open), par uske liye purana likha hua code na change karna pade (Closed).
lessons.analogy: Maan lo ek Extension Board hai. Agar tumhe naya charger lagana hai, toh tum extension board ko khol ke uski taar nahi kaat te (Modification). Tum bas ek naye socket mein plug daal dete ho (Extension).
lessons.why: Kyunki chalti hui cheez ko chhedne se bugs aate hain. Agar purana tested code touch nahi hoga, toh production mein phatne ke chances zero hain.

lessons.name: LSP — Liskov Substitution: subtypes must replace base types
lessons.desc: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without affecting correctness. Subtypes must satisfy the base type contract.
lessons.q: Why is the Square-Rectangle problem the classic example of violating LSP? How do preconditions and postconditions relate?
lessons.qsub: Violating LSP breaks polymorphism. Classic violation: Square extends Rectangle (width/height invariants differ). Design by Contract approach.
lessons.what: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) kehta hai ki agar Class B, Class A se inherit karti hai, toh program mein jahan bhi Class A use ho rahi ho, wahan Class B ko rakh dene se program fatna nahi chahiye.
lessons.analogy: Agar ek toy duck duck ki tarah dikhti hai aur quack bhi karti hai, par usko batteries chahiye, toh tum usko aslee ducks ke saath pond (talaab) mein nahi chhod sakte. Wo short-circuit ho jayegi (LSP violation).
lessons.why: Kyunki agar subclass parent ke rules (contracts) todti hai, toh polymorphism fail ho jayega aur client code mein bohot saare if (obj instanceof B) dalne padenge.
gotchas: Classic Example: Square extends Rectangle. Ek Rectangle mein width aur height alag change ho sakti hain. Agar Square use karoge, toh area calculation fail ho jayegi kyunki Square mein dono same hone zaroori hain.

lessons.name: ISP — Interface Segregation: small focused interfaces
lessons.desc: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Large interfaces should be split into smaller, more specific ones.
lessons.q: How does Interface Segregation reduce coupling and prevent dummy method implementations?
lessons.qsub: Fat interfaces lead to coupling and empty method implementations. Segregation reduces surprise and makes systems easier to understand.
lessons.what: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) kehta hai ki clients ko un methods pe depend karne ke liye majboor mat karo jo wo use nahi karte. Ek bade (fat) interface se behtar hai chhote-chhote specific interfaces banana.
lessons.analogy: Socho ek restaurant ka menu hai. Ek hi menu mein Italian, Chinese, aur South Indian sab hai. Agar tumhe dosa khana hai, toh tum poore menu mein dhoondte rahoge. Iski jagah 3 alag chote menus hone chahiye.

lessons.name: DIP — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions
lessons.desc: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details.
lessons.q: How does Dependency Injection implement the Dependency Inversion Principle? What problem does it solve?
lessons.qsub: Inverting dependencies decouples policy from implementation. Dependency Injection is the most common technique to achieve DIP.
terms: Chhote utilities ya tools (e.g. MySQLDatabase, SmtpEmail)
lessons.what: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) kehta hai ki High-level classes ko Low-level classes pe direct depend nahi karna chahiye. Dono ko abstractions (interfaces) pe depend karna chahiye.
lessons.analogy:
Socho tum ek Lamp (High-level) banate ho, usme tumne wall socket ke taar direct baandh diye (Low-level). Ab ye lamp kisi dusre plug mein nahi lag sakta.

DIP kehta hai ki Lamp mein ek Plug hona chahiye (Abstraction), aur wall mein ek Socket hona chahiye. Ab dono ek contract ke through connected hain aur aasani se decouple ho sakte hain.
lessons.why: Direct depend karne se classes tight couple ho jati hain. Agar tum MySQLDatabase use kar rahe ho aur kal ko MongoDB pe jana pade, toh pura high-level logic fat jayega.

lessons.name: Composition over Inheritance — prefer has-a over is-a when possible
lessons.desc: Favor has-a relationships over is-a relationships. Achieve reuse by composing objects, not by inheriting from a base class.
lessons.q: Why does composition provide more flexibility than inheritance at runtime? How does the Decorator pattern demonstrate this?
lessons.qsub: Inheritance creates tight coupling and fragile hierarchies. Composition is more flexible, allows runtime behavior changes, and avoids the yo-yo problem.
terms: Ek class se extend karke nayi class banana
Chhote-chhote parts (objects) ko jod kar ek bada object banana
lessons.what: Composition over Inheritance ek rule of thumb hai jo kehta hai ki code reuse karne ke liye objects ko aapas mein jodna (compose karna) better hota hai, bjaye ek base class se inherit karne ke.
lessons.analogy:
Socho tumhe ek custom gaadi banani hai.

Inheritance approach: Tum ek BaseCar lete ho, usse SportsCar banate ho, usse SunroofSportsCar banate ho, usse RedSunroofSportsCar. Ye chain bohot gandi ho jati hai.

Composition approach: Tumhare paas ek Car ka dabba hai, jisme tum alag se Engine daalte ho, Paint daalte ho, aur Roof daalte ho. Tum kabhi bhi engine swap kar sakte ho.
lessons.why:
Inheritance tight coupling create karti hai. Agar BaseCar mein change aaya toh saari cars affect hongi. Plus inheritance static hoti hai (run-time pe change nahi kar sakte).

Composition bohot flexible hoti hai aur runtime pe behavior badalne deti hai.

lessons.name: Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge) — talk only to immediate friends
lessons.desc: A method should only call methods on: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, its own fields. Dont talk to strangers (method chaining like a.getB().getC().do()).
lessons.q: Why does the Law of Demeter reduce coupling? What is the trade-off of following it too strictly?
lessons.qsub: Reduces coupling between components. Following LoD creates more maintainable code but can lead to many wrapper/delegate methods.
lessons.what: Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge) kehta hai ki ek object ko apne aas-paas ki duniya (dusre objects ke internals) ke baare mein kam se kam pata hona chahiye.
lessons.analogy: Tum ek dukaan pe gaye chips lene. Tum dukaandaar ko paise doge (Method call). Tum dukaandaar ki jeb mein haath daal ke khud uska wallet nikal kar wahan se paise nahi katoge. Code mein aisi harkat mat karo!
lessons.why: Kyunki lambi chaining a.getB().getC().doThing() se classes ek dusre se strongly couple ho jati hain. Agar B ki internal structure change hui, toh A ka code break ho jayega.

lessons.name: DRY, KISS, YAGNI — dont repeat, keep simple, avoid over-engineering
lessons.desc: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid), YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). Three principles guiding pragmatic software design.
lessons.q: How can over-applying DRY lead to premature abstraction? When does YAGNI apply to design patterns?
lessons.qsub: DRY reduces duplication cost. KISS favors simplicity over cleverness. YAGNI prevents over-engineering for hypothetical future needs.
lessons.what:
Teen basic rules jo har developer ko pata hone chahiye:

  • DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Code copy-paste mat karo. Same logic 2 jagah hai toh usko ek function mein dalo.
  • KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): Code ko over-engineer mat karo. Aasan code likho jo kal ko padh sako.
  • YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): "Shayad future mein zaroorat pade" soch kar aaj aisi features mat banao jo abhi required nahi hain.

lessons.name: Coupling & Cohesion — low coupling, high cohesion
lessons.desc: Coupling measures how dependent one module is on another. Cohesion measures how focused the responsibilities within a module are. Aim for low coupling, high cohesion.
lessons.q: Why is low coupling and high cohesion the sweet spot for software maintainability and testability?
lessons.qsub: Low coupling = changes are isolated. High cohesion = classes are focused. Together they make systems more maintainable, testable, and understandable.
lessons.what:
Coupling: Do classes ek dusre pe kitna depend karti hain. (Aim: Low Coupling - Classes azaad honi chahiye).

Cohesion: Ek class ke methods aur variables ka aapas mein kitna lena-dena hai. (Aim: High Cohesion - Class ka ek hi focus hona chahiye, SRP jaisa).

lessons.name: Tell-Dont-Ask — command objects what to do, dont query state
lessons.desc: Tell objects what to do rather than asking about their state and then deciding. Encapsulate behavior with data.
lessons.q: How does Tell-Dont-Ask preserve encapsulation and eliminate anemic domain models? Give a code example.
lessons.qsub: Preserves encapsulation and prevents decision-making being scattered across the codebase. Related to "feature envy" code smell in reverse.
lessons.what: Tell-Don't-Ask ka principle kehta hai ki object se data maang (ask) kar khud decision lene ke bjaye, object ko apna kaam khud karne ko bolo (tell).
lessons.analogy: Tum waiter se puchte ho (Ask): "Kya kitchen khula hai? Kya bread hai? Toh fir mere liye sandwich bana do." Iski jagah tum bas kehte ho (Tell): "Mere liye ek sandwich lao." Waiter khud check karega sab kuch.

lessons.name: Singleton — ensure one instance, global access point. Thread-safety considerations.
lessons.desc: Singleton ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access. Thread-safety through eager initialization, synchronized getInstance, or Bill Pugh inner class.
lessons.q: How do you implement a thread-safe Singleton in Java? Why is enum Singleton considered the most robust approach?
lessons.qsub: Useful for shared resources (logging, configuration, thread pools). Overused / considered an anti-pattern — makes testing difficult and introduces global state.
terms: Kahi se bhi us object ko access karne ka tareeqa
lessons.what: Singleton Pattern ye ensure karta hai ki ek class ka pure application mein sirf aur sirf ek hi instance (object) banega, aur usko access karne ka ek global tareeqa hoga.
lessons.analogy: Jaise kisi desh ka ek hi Prime Minister hota hai. Chahe tum Delhi se bulao ya Mumbai se, PM wahi ek banda hoga. Naya PM create nahi kar sakte, jo existing hai ussi se baat karni padegi.
lessons.why: Kuch cheezein system mein ek hi honi chahiye, jaise Database Connection Pool, Logger, ya Configuration settings. Agar har jagah naya connection open karoge toh system crash ho jayega aur memory bhar jayegi.

lessons.name: Factory Method — define interface for creating objects, subclasses decide instantiation
lessons.desc: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. The Creator class defers instantiation to subclasses.
lessons.q: How does Factory Method decouple clients from concrete types and enable the Open/Closed Principle?
lessons.qsub: Decouples the client from concrete types. Enables the Open/Closed principle — new types can be added without modifying existing code.
terms: Wo class jisme factory method hota hai
Wo object jo factory method banata hai
lessons.what: Factory Method ek creational pattern hai jo object create karne ka logic ek separate method mein daal deta hai. Subclasses us method ko override karke decide kar sakti hain ki kis type ka object banana hai.
lessons.analogy: Maan lo ek Logistics company hai jo Delivery karti hai. Shuru mein unke paas sirf Trucks the, toh unhone "TruckDelivery" class banai. Kal ko unhone Ships (samundar se) delivery chalu kardi. Factory pattern kehta hai: "Transport create karne ki factory alag banao. Zameen pe ho toh RoadLogistics (jo Truck banayega), aur paani pe ho toh SeaLogistics (jo Ship banayega)."
lessons.why: Objects ko directly new Keyword se banane se tumhari class us specific object se tightly couple ho jati hai. Factory use karke tum "kya banana hai" ye decision subclasses par chhod dete ho, jisse naye products add karna bohot aasan ho jata hai (OCP follow hota hai).

lessons.name: Abstract Factory — create families of related objects without concrete classes
lessons.desc: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. A "factory of factories".
lessons.q: When would you use Abstract Factory over Factory Method? How does it ensure product compatibility?
lessons.qsub: Ensures products from the same family are used together. Switching families (e.g., different UI themes) is done by swapping the factory implementation.
lessons.what: Abstract Factory patterns ka ek level up hai. Ye ek factory of factories hai. Ye tumhe related objects ki poori "Family" (theme) banane deta hai bina unki concrete classes specify kiye.
lessons.analogy:
Socho tumhe ek Furniture ki factory setup karni hai. Tumhare paas do Themes hain: "Modern" aur "Victorian".

Modern Factory tumhe: ModernChair, ModernSofa, ModernTable degi.
Victorian Factory tumhe: VicChair, VicSofa, VicTable degi.
Abstract Factory ensure karti hai ki tum galti se ModernChair ke saath VictorianTable match na kar do. Ek factory chuno, aur usse related saara furniture mangwa lo.
lessons.why: Jab tumhare paas products ki alag-alag families hon (jaise macOS UI components vs Windows UI components) aur tum chahte ho ki system us family ke bahar mix-and-match na kare.

cons: Agar tumhe naya product type add karna ho (jaise Scrollbar), toh saari ki saari factories (Abstract + Mac + Win) modify karni padengi.

lessons.name: Builder — separate construction of complex objects from representation
lessons.desc: Builder separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. The same construction process can create different representations via a director + builder interface.
lessons.q: How does Builder solve the telescoping constructor problem? What makes it different from Factory?
lessons.qsub: Ideal for objects with many optional parameters (telescoping constructor problem). Provides fluent API and immutable objects.
lessons.what: Builder Pattern complex objects ko step-by-step banane (construct) mein madad karta hai. Constructor mein 10 parameters pass karne ki jagah (Telescoping Constructor Anti-pattern), hum ek Builder object use karte hain.
lessons.analogy: Subway ya Burger King mein jaake burger order karna. Tum sidha "Burger dedo jisme paneer ho, tomato ho par onion na ho, mayo double ho" nahi bolte ek saans mein. Tum step by step bolte ho: "Bread do -> Paneer dalo -> Onion hatao -> Mayo dalo". Builder pattern wahi hai.
lessons.why: Jab object ko banane ka process (creation) bohot complex ho aur usmein bohot saare optional parameters hon. Constructor arguments lambe hone lagte hain jisko padhna impossible ho jata hai: new House(true, false, 4, true, null, false).
pros: Bohot saare optional parameters wale objects aasani se ban jate hain
Code padhne mein (Method chaining / fluent interface ki wajah se) maza aata hai
Immutability: Ek baar build() ho gaya toh object lock (freeze) ho jata hai
cons: Har class ke liye ek nayi Builder class banani padti hai (Boilerplate)

lessons.name: Prototype — clone existing objects instead of creating new from scratch
lessons.desc: Prototype creates new objects by cloning/copying an existing instance (the prototype). Avoids costly creation from scratch, especially when object initialization is expensive.
lessons.q: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy in the Prototype pattern? When is it useful?
lessons.qsub: Useful when object creation is expensive and you need many similar objects. Shallow vs deep copy considerations are critical.

lessons.name: Object Pool — reuse objects that are expensive to create (connections, threads)
lessons.desc: Object Pool manages a reusable set of initialized objects. Clients borrow from the pool and return objects instead of creating/destroying them.
lessons.q: What problems does Object Pool solve beyond performance? How do you handle stale/broken objects in the pool?
lessons.qsub: Avoids expensive allocation/deallocation. Controls resource usage (max pool size). Requires careful thread-safety and handling of broken/expired objects.

lessons.name: Adapter — convert interface of a class to another interface clients expect
lessons.desc: Adapter converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect. Lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise due to incompatible interfaces.
lessons.q: What is the difference between class adapter and object adapter? Why is composition preferred?
lessons.qsub: Integrate legacy or third-party code without modification. Two variants: class adapter (inheritance) and object adapter (composition). Composition is preferred.
lessons.what: Adapter Pattern ek structural design pattern hai jo do aisi classes ko saath mein kaam karne deta hai jinke interfaces aapas mein match nahi hote (incompatible interfaces).
lessons.analogy: Maan lo tumhare paas ek Indian plug (3-pin) hai, par tum kisi foreign country mein gaye jahan sirf 2-pin ke sockets hain. Ab tum plug ki taar nahi kaatoge, tum ek Travel Adapter kharidoge jo 3-pin ko 2-pin mein convert kar dega. Code mein bhi adapter yahi kaam karta hai.
lessons.why: Jab tum kisi 3rd-party library, legacy code, ya aisi class ko use karna chahte ho jiska interface tumhare naye system se mail (match) nahi khata, aur tum us purane code ko modify nahi kar sakte (ya nahi karna chahte).

lessons.name: Bridge — decouple abstraction from implementation so they vary independently
lessons.desc: Bridge decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently. Avoids permanent binding between abstraction and implementation at compile time.
lessons.q: How does Bridge prevent the Cartesian product explosion of subclasses? Give a real-world example.
lessons.qsub: Prevents explosion of classes when you have multiple abstractions and multiple implementations. "Bridge" the gap when both can change.

lessons.name: Composite — compose objects into tree structures, treat individuals uniformly
lessons.desc: Composite composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly via a common interface.
lessons.q: How does Composite simplify client code when dealing with tree structures like file systems or UI components?
lessons.qsub: Simplifies client code when dealing with tree structures. The client calls the same method regardless of whether it's a leaf or a composite.

lessons.name: Decorator — attach responsibilities to objects dynamically (wrapper)
lessons.desc: Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.
lessons.q: How is Decorator more flexible than inheritance for adding behavior? How do decorators stack?
lessons.qsub: Add behavior without modifying the original class. More flexible than inheritance (choose which decorators at runtime). Each decorator adds its own behavior.
lessons.what: Decorator Pattern ek structural pattern hai jo objects mein runtime par nayi behaviors (features) add karne deta hai, bina unki class ko modify kiye ya subclass banaye.
lessons.analogy: Socho tumne ek simple Pizza kharida. Ab tumhe usme extra cheese chahiye (add behavior), fir tumhe usme olives chahiye (add more behavior). Tum har combination ke liye nayi class (ExtraCheeseOlivesPizza) nahi banate. Tum original pizza ko "Decorator" (toppings) se wrap karte ho.
lessons.why: Kyunki inheritance se behaviors add karne mein "Class Explosion" ho jata hai. Agar 5 features hain, toh unke combinations ke liye 25 classes ban jayengi. Decorator pattern Composition use karke is problem ko solve karta hai.
pros: Inheritance ka sub-classing explosion khatam
Single Responsibility Principle: Ek lambi class mein saara features dalne ke bjaye har feature ki alag decorator class
cons: Bohot saari chhoti-chhoti classes ban jati hain (MilkDecorator, SugarDecorator, VanillaDecorator etc.)
Wrap karte waqt code lamba lagta hai: new A(new B(new C()))
gotchas: Decorator aur Proxy mein log confuse hote hain. Decorator nayi "behavior" add karta hai. Proxy bas access "control" karta hai (wo generally naya kaam add nahi karta).

lessons.name: Facade — provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
lessons.desc: Facade provides a unified, simplified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use.
lessons.q: How does Facade differ from Mediator? Does Facade hide the subsystem or just simplify access?
lessons.qsub: Reduces complexity for the client. Decouples client code from subsystem components. Does NOT hide the subsystem — clients can still access lower-level APIs.
lessons.what: Facade Pattern (Padho: Fa-saad) ek library, framework ya complex system ko access karne ke liye ek bohot hi simplified interface (ya front-face) deta hai.
lessons.analogy: Socho tum Amazon pe order place karte ho. Tum sirf ek button dabate ho "Buy Now". Piche warehouse, logistics, inventory check, payment processing, invoice generation, bank confirmation — ye sab kitna complex hai, usse tumhe koi matlab nahi. "Buy Now" button ek Facade hai us complex system ke liye.
lessons.why: Agar tumhare code ko dusre framework ki 10 classes ke saath baat karni padegi, toh tight coupling ho jayegi. Facade ek deewar/shield ban jata hai. Tumhara code sirf Facade se baat karta hai, aur Facade baaki 10 classes ko handle karta hai.

gotchas: Facade aur Adapter mein farq: Adapter existing interface ko *convert* karta hai (uski complexity nahi kam karta). Facade naya, *simplified* interface banata hai.

lessons.name: Flyweight — share fine-grained objects to support large numbers efficiently
lessons.desc: Flyweight minimizes memory usage by sharing as much data as possible with similar objects. Intrinsic state (shared) vs extrinsic state (passed in context).
lessons.q: How do you decide what goes into intrinsic vs extrinsic state in the Flyweight pattern? Give an example.
lessons.qsub: Critical when dealing with large numbers of fine-grained objects. The state split is the key insight — what can be shared vs what must be external.

lessons.name: Proxy — provide a surrogate or placeholder to control access
lessons.desc: Proxy provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access. Variants: virtual proxy (lazy load), protection proxy (access control), remote proxy.
lessons.q: What are the four variants of Proxy and what problem does each solve? How does Proxy differ from Decorator?
lessons.qsub: Add a level of indirection for separation of concerns. Each variant solves a different problem: lazy init, security, remote invocation, or logging.
lessons.what: Proxy Pattern kisi dusre object ke liye ek surrogate (ya substitute) provide karta hai, taaki us object ke access ko control kiya ja sake.
lessons.analogy: Socho kisi bade CEO se tum direct nahi mil sakte. Tumhe uske Secretary (Proxy) se appointment leni padegi. Secretary pehle check karegi ki tumhare paas zaruri reason hai ya nahi, aur uske baad hi tum CEO tak pahunchoge. Proxy access ko filter/control kar raha hai.
lessons.why: Kuch objects bohot heavy hote hain (jaise DB connection, ya badi images), toh Proxy unhe tab tak load nahi hone deta jab tak zarurat na ho (Lazy Initialization). Ya phir security (Access control), Caching, aur logging ke liye Proxy pattern lagaya jata hai.
pros: Original object ko bina chhede (OCP) hum nayi capabilities add kar sakte hain (e.g. caching)
Heavy objects ke lifecycle (creation/destruction) ko control kiya ja sakta hai

lessons.name: Chain of Responsibility — pass requests along a chain of handlers
lessons.desc: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides to process the request or pass it to the next handler.
lessons.q: How does Chain of Responsibility decouple the sender from the receiver? What happens if no handler processes the request?
lessons.qsub: Avoids coupling the sender to a specific receiver. Multiple handlers get a chance to process the request. Common in logging frameworks, middleware pipelines.

lessons.name: Command — encapsulate a request as an object (undo/redo, queue, log)
lessons.desc: Command encapsulates a request as an object, allowing parameterization, queuing, logging, undo/redo. Contains all info needed to perform an action.
lessons.q: How does Command enable undo/redo functionality? What is the relationship between Command and Memento?
lessons.qsub: Enables delayed execution, queuing, and undoable operations. Foundation for transactional behavior and macro recording.

lessons.name: Interpreter — define grammar + interpreter for language sentences
lessons.desc: Interpreter defines a grammar for a language and an interpreter that uses the representation to interpret sentences in the language.
lessons.q: When is Interpreter appropriate vs using a parser generator? What are the trade-offs?
lessons.qsub: Useful for parsing simple languages or expressions (regex, SQL, arithmetic). For complex grammars, use parser generators instead.

lessons.name: Iterator — provide sequential access to elements without exposing internals
lessons.desc: Iterator provides a way to access elements of a collection sequentially without exposing the underlying representation.
lessons.q: How does Iterator separate traversal logic from the collection? Why is it useful for different collection types?
lessons.qsub: Simplifies collection interface and enables multiple simultaneous traversals. The client doesn't need to know if the collection is an array, tree, or hash map.

lessons.name: Mediator — reduce chaotic coupling by centralizing communication
lessons.desc: Mediator reduces chaotic communication between multiple objects by introducing a mediator object that centralizes interactions.
lessons.q: What is the trade-off of Mediator? How does it risk becoming a God Object and how do you prevent that?
lessons.qsub: Prevents many-to-many communication (simplified to one-to-many). Reduces coupling at the cost of a more complex mediator.

lessons.name: Memento — capture and restore object state without violating encapsulation
lessons.desc: Memento captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later without violating encapsulation.
lessons.q: How does Memento preserve encapsulation while enabling undo/checkpoint functionality? What are the three roles?
lessons.qsub: Enables undo/redo, checkpoint/rollback, and snapshots without exposing internal structure. The caretaker never accesses memento contents.

lessons.name: Observer — define one-to-many dependency; when one changes, all dependents notified
lessons.desc: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency between objects. When the subject changes state, all its dependents (observers) are notified and updated automatically.
lessons.q: What is the difference between push model and pull model in Observer? When would you use each?
lessons.qsub: Essential for event-driven systems, UI updates, and reactive programming. The subject doesn't need to know observer details.

lessons.name: State — alter behavior when internal state changes (state machine)
lessons.desc: State allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object appears to change its class. Each state is a separate class.
lessons.q: How does State eliminate complex if/else switch statements? How does it differ from Strategy?
lessons.qsub: Eliminates complex if/else or switch state machines. Adding a new state is just adding a new class — OCP compliant.

lessons.name: Strategy — define family of algorithms, make them interchangeable
lessons.desc: Strategy defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. The algorithm can vary independently from clients that use it.
lessons.q: How does Strategy enable selecting algorithms at runtime? Give an example where it replaces complex conditional logic.
lessons.qsub: Enables selecting algorithms at runtime. Cleaner alternative to conditional logic for algorithm selection. Follows Open/Closed principle.

lessons.name: Template Method — define skeleton of algorithm, subclasses override steps
lessons.desc: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses. Subclasses redefine certain steps without changing the algorithm's structure.
lessons.q: What is the Hollywood Principle and how does Template Method embody it? What are hook methods?
lessons.qsub: Reuses the invariant parts of an algorithm while letting subclasses define the variant parts. Hollywood Principle: "Don't call us, we'll call you."

lessons.name: Visitor — separate algorithm from object structure (Double Dispatch)
lessons.desc: Visitor lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates. Separates algorithm from object structure via Double Dispatch.
lessons.q: What is Double Dispatch and how does Visitor achieve it? When is Visitor appropriate vs when does it become a maintenance burden?
lessons.qsub: When you have a stable object structure but need to add many operations. Classic example: AST nodes with type-checking, code generation, optimization.

lessons.name: Active Object — decouple method execution from invocation (async + scheduler)
lessons.desc: Active Object decouples method execution from method invocation. Each object has its own thread of control and a scheduler that queues invocation requests.
lessons.q: How does Active Object enable asynchronous processing without explicit thread management? How does it relate to the Actor model?
lessons.qsub: Enables asynchronous processing without explicit thread management. The caller doesn't block — results come back via futures or callbacks.

lessons.name: Balking — only execute action if object is in appropriate state
lessons.desc: Balking Pattern prevents an action if the object is in an inappropriate state. If the guard condition fails, the method returns immediately (bails out).
lessons.q: How does Balking provide a simple alternative to blocking for handling race conditions? Give a real-world example.
lessons.qsub: Simple way to handle race conditions without blocking. "If not ready, just return/throw." Used when the work is only meaningful in specific states.

lessons.name: Barrier — synchronize a group of threads at a common point
lessons.desc: Barrier synchronizes multiple threads at a common point. All threads must arrive at the barrier before any can proceed past it.
lessons.q: How does CyclicBarrier differ from CountDownLatch? When would you use a barrier for parallel algorithms?
lessons.qsub: Useful for parallel algorithms where all threads must complete one phase before starting the next (e.g., parallel sort merge phases).

lessons.name: Double-Checked Locking — reduce lock overhead by checking before acquiring
lessons.desc: Double-Checked Locking reduces the overhead of acquiring a lock by first testing the locking criterion without acquiring the lock.
lessons.q: Why does Double-Checked Locking require the volatile keyword in Java? What problem occurs without it?
lessons.qsub: Optimization for lazy initialization in multithreaded code. In Java, requires volatile to prevent instruction reordering issues.

lessons.name: Future / Promise — placeholder for async result (CompletableFuture)
lessons.desc: Future/Promise represents a placeholder for a result that hasn't been computed yet. The future is returned immediately; the caller can check, block, or attach callbacks.
lessons.q: How does CompletableFuture enable non-blocking asynchronous composition without callback nesting?
lessons.qsub: Enables non-blocking asynchronous programming. CompletableFuture chains transformations without callback nesting.

lessons.name: Producer-Consumer — decouple producers from consumers via a buffer
lessons.desc: Producer-Consumer decouples producers (create data) from consumers (process data) using a shared buffer/queue.
lessons.q: How does BlockingQueue simplify Producer-Consumer? What happens if the buffer is full or empty?
lessons.qsub: Solves the classic synchronization problem. Producers and consumers can operate at different rates. Buffer absorbs bursts of production.

lessons.name: Read-Write Lock — allow concurrent reads, exclusive writes
lessons.desc: Read-Write Lock allows multiple threads to read simultaneously but requires exclusive access for writes. Improves concurrency for read-heavy workloads.
lessons.q: Why is Read-Write Lock better than a regular mutex for read-heavy workloads? What is the risk of writer starvation?
lessons.qsub: Read operations don't conflict with each other, only with writes. Using a regular mutex would unnecessarily block readers.

lessons.name: Thread Pool — manage reusable threads for executing tasks
lessons.desc: Thread Pool manages a reusable pool of worker threads. Tasks are submitted to a queue, and idle workers pick up tasks.
lessons.q: What are the different types of thread pools (fixed, cached, scheduled)? What is a rejection policy?
lessons.qsub: Thread creation is expensive. Pool limits maximum concurrency, prevents resource exhaustion, and provides management (monitoring, tuning).

lessons.name: Thread-Local Storage — isolate data per thread (no synchronization needed)
lessons.desc: Thread-Local Storage provides each thread with its own copy of a variable. No synchronization needed because each thread has exclusive access to its own copy.
lessons.q: How does ThreadLocal eliminate contention for per-thread data? What is the memory leak risk in thread pools?
lessons.qsub: Eliminates contention entirely for per-thread data. Common for request-scoped context (user ID, transaction ID) in web servers.

lessons.name: MVC — Model-View-Controller: separate data, UI, and input handling
lessons.desc: MVC separates an application into three components: Model (data + business logic), View (UI presentation), Controller (handles input and updates Model/View).
lessons.q: How does MVC enable multiple views of the same model and testable business logic independent of UI?
lessons.qsub: Separation of concerns enables parallel development, multiple views of the same model, and testable business logic independent of UI.

lessons.name: MVP / MVVM — presentation patterns for testable UIs
lessons.desc: MVP/MVVM are presentation patterns for testable UIs. MVP: View is passive, Presenter contains logic. MVVM: View binds to ViewModel via data binding.
lessons.q: Compare MVP and MVVM. When would you choose one over the other for testability and boilerplate?
lessons.qsub: MVP: maximal testability (Presenter has no UI dependency). MVVM: less boilerplate via data binding.

lessons.name: Layered Architecture — horizontal layers (presentation, business, persistence)
lessons.desc: Layered Architecture organizes code into horizontal layers (presentation, business, persistence). Each layer has a specific responsibility and communicates only with adjacent layers.
lessons.q: What is the sinkhole anti-pattern in Layered Architecture? When does layered architecture become a monolithic problem?
lessons.qsub: Separation of concerns, each layer can be developed/tested independently. But can lead to monolithic designs and "sinkhole" anti-pattern.

lessons.name: Microservices — decompose by business capability, independently deployable
lessons.desc: Microservices decomposes an application into small, independently deployable services organized around business capabilities.
lessons.q: What are the trade-offs of microservices vs monoliths? How do you handle distributed transactions?
lessons.qsub: Independent scaling, deployment, and technology choices. Better fault isolation but introduces distributed systems complexity.

lessons.name: Event-Driven Architecture — components communicate via events (pub/sub)
lessons.desc: Event-Driven Architecture components communicate through events. Producers emit events, consumers react. Can use message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
lessons.q: What are the challenges of event-driven architecture in terms of tracing and debugging? Compare pub/sub to point-to-point.
lessons.qsub: Highly decoupled, asynchronous, and scalable. Enables real-time processing and event sourcing. Harder to trace and debug.

lessons.name: CQRS — separate command (write) and query (read) models
lessons.desc: CQRS separates read operations (queries) from write operations (commands). They may use different models and even different data stores.
lessons.q: How does CQRS optimize reads and writes independently? Why is it often paired with Event Sourcing?
lessons.qsub: Optimizes reads and writes independently. Reads can use denormalized projections, writes use normalized models.

lessons.name: Event Sourcing — store state changes as sequence of events
lessons.desc: Event Sourcing stores state changes as a sequence of events. Current state is derived by replaying all events. Events are the single source of truth.
lessons.q: How does Event Sourcing provide a complete audit trail? What is the snapshot optimization for large event streams?
lessons.qsub: Complete audit trail, temporal queries, ability to rebuild state at any point. Complex to query current state without projections.

lessons.name: Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters — core logic isolated from external systems
lessons.desc: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core business logic from external systems. Core defines ports (interfaces); adapters implement them.
lessons.q: How does Hexagonal Architecture make core logic testable without infrastructure? What are driving vs driven adapters?
lessons.qsub: Core logic is pure and testable without infrastructure. Swap databases, UIs, or external services by writing new adapters.

lessons.name: Domain-Driven Design — ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, aggregates
lessons.desc: Domain-Driven Design focuses on modeling the domain first. Uses ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, aggregates, entities, value objects.
lessons.q: What is a bounded context and an aggregate in DDD? How does ubiquitous language bridge domain experts and developers?
lessons.qsub: Aligns software with business needs. Ubiquitous language bridges domain experts and developers.

lessons.name: Repository Pattern — mediate between domain and data mapping layers
lessons.desc: Repository Pattern mediates between the domain and data mapping layers. Acts like an in-memory collection of domain objects.
lessons.q: How does Repository abstract persistence details away from domain code? How does it simplify unit testing?
lessons.qsub: Provides a clean separation of concerns. Domain code doesn't know about databases, ORMs, or file storage. Makes unit testing easy.

lessons.name: Unit of Work — maintain list of changed objects, commit as transaction
lessons.desc: Unit of Work maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction. Coordinates writing changes and resolves concurrency problems.
lessons.q: How does Unit of Work ensure transactional consistency? What is the relationship with Repository?
lessons.qsub: Ensures transactional consistency. Multiple changes are written as one atomic unit. Performance improvements by batching writes.

lessons.name: Parking Lot System
lessons.desc: Design a multi-level parking lot handling vehicle entry/exit, spot assignment, fee calculation. Patterns: Singleton, Factory, Strategy.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a parking lot system. Model different vehicle types, spot assignment, and fee calculation.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle a full lot scenario?

lessons.name: Elevator Control System
lessons.desc: Design elevator logic with request handling, direction strategy, door operations. Patterns: State, Command, Observer.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design an elevator control system. Handle concurrent requests from multiple floors.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle emergency stop?

lessons.name: Vending Machine
lessons.desc: Design product selection, payment processing, change calculation, and inventory management. Patterns: State, Factory.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a vending machine with product selection, payment, and change calculation.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle out-of-stock and exact change scenarios?

lessons.name: Chess / Game Design
lessons.desc: Model pieces with movement rules, board state, player turns, check/checkmate detection. Patterns: Composite, Command, Strategy, Memento.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a chess game system with move validation, undo/redo, and AI opponents.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle special moves like castling and en passant?

lessons.name: Library Management System
lessons.desc: Design books, members, borrowing/returning, fines management. Patterns: Repository, Singleton, Factory.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a library management system with borrowing, returns, reservations, and fine calculation.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle due dates and overlapping reservations?

lessons.name: Logger Framework
lessons.desc: Design a flexible logging system with multiple appenders, log levels, formatting. Patterns: Singleton, Chain of Resp, Factory.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a logging framework with configurable log levels, appenders, and formatting.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you add a new appender without modifying existing code?

lessons.name: Pub-Sub Message Queue
lessons.desc: Design a topic-based publish/subscribe system. Patterns: Observer, Singleton, Thread Pool.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a pub-sub message queue with topics, subscribers, and async delivery.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you guarantee at-least-once delivery?

lessons.name: ATM / Banking System
lessons.desc: Model card authentication, account types, transactions. Patterns: State, Command, Chain of Resp.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design an ATM system with card authentication, PIN verification, and transaction processing.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle rollback on transaction failure?

lessons.name: Tic Tac Toe
lessons.desc: Design the board, players, win condition checking. Patterns: Strategy, Factory.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a Tic Tac Toe game supporting human vs human and human vs computer modes.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you detect a draw?

lessons.name: Task Management (Jira-like)
lessons.desc: Create stories/tasks, assign, transition through workflow states. Patterns: State, Command, Observer, Composite.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a task management system with workflow states, assignments, and notifications.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you model sub-tasks and epics?

lessons.name: Rate Limiter
lessons.desc: Limit API requests per client within time windows. Patterns: Strategy, Proxy, Factory.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a rate limiter supporting multiple algorithms (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window).
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle distributed rate limiting?

lessons.name: Chat System
lessons.desc: Design real-time messaging with rooms, private messages, user status. Patterns: Observer, Mediator, Command, Singleton.
lessons.q: LLD Problem: Design a real-time chat system with rooms, private messaging, and presence tracking.
lessons.qsub: Walk through your class design, key patterns used, and tradeoffs. How do you handle message ordering?

lessons.name: God Object — one class knows/does too much (violates SRP)
lessons.desc: God Object — a single class that knows too much or does too much. It has too many responsibilities and becomes extremely hard to maintain.
lessons.q: How does the God Object violate SRP? What refactoring steps would you take to fix one?
lessons.qsub: Classic SRP violation. God objects are a code smell — refactor by extracting responsibilities into focused classes.

lessons.name: Spaghetti Code — no clear structure, GOTO-like logic
lessons.desc: Spaghetti Code — code with no clear structure, characterized by excessive nesting, and unpredictable control flow.
lessons.q: How does deep nesting and scattered state mutations create spaghetti code? How do design patterns help?
lessons.qsub: Unmaintainable and bug-prone. Deeply nested callbacks, scattered state mutations, and convoluted conditionals create the same problem as GOTO.

lessons.name: Golden Hammer — applying a favorite pattern everywhere
lessons.desc: Golden Hammer — treating every problem as a nail because you have a favorite pattern. Over-applying a pattern that worked well elsewhere.
lessons.q: When does using a design pattern become over-engineering? How does YAGNI relate to the Golden Hammer?
lessons.qsub: Patterns are solutions in context, not universal remedies. The right pattern depends on the specific problem characteristics.

lessons.name: Callback Hell — deeply nested callbacks, use Promises/async patterns
lessons.desc: Callback Hell (Pyramid of Doom) — deeply nested callbacks that make code hard to read, reason about, and debug.
lessons.q: How do Promises and async/await solve Callback Hell? What design pattern can help organize callback chains?
lessons.qsub: Creates unmanageable code structure with complex error handling. Modern alternatives (Promises, async/await) flatten the pyramid.

lessons.name: Singleton Abuse — overusing global state, testing difficulties
lessons.desc: Singleton Abuse — overusing the Singleton pattern leads to global state that is hard to test, reason about, and maintain.
lessons.q: Why are Singletons considered an anti-pattern in many contexts? What is the preferred alternative?
lessons.qsub: Singletons create implicit shared global state. Code with Singletons is hard to unit test and creates invisible coupling.

lessons.name: Yo-Yo Problem — deep inheritance hierarchies making code hard to follow
lessons.desc: Yo-Yo Problem — deep inheritance hierarchies where understanding behavior requires jumping up and down the hierarchy repeatedly.
lessons.q: How does deep inheritance create the fragile base class problem? How does composition over inheritance solve this?
lessons.qsub: Over-reliance on inheritance creates fragile hierarchies. A change at the top can ripple through the entire system.

lessons.name: Premature Optimization — optimizing before understanding the real bottleneck
lessons.desc: Premature Optimization — optimizing code before understanding the actual bottleneck. Knuth: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil."
lessons.q: Why is premature optimization problematic even when the optimization seems obvious? What is the correct approach?
lessons.qsub: Optimization adds complexity. Without profiling, you might optimize the wrong thing. Write clean, correct code first, then profile, then optimize.

lessons.name: "Design a system to support multiple notification channels" (Strategy + Observer)
lessons.desc: Design a system that sends notifications via email, SMS, push, and in-app. Strategy (channel algorithms), Observer (trigger events), Factory (channel creation).
lessons.q: Design a notification system that supports email, SMS, push, and in-app notifications. How do you add a new channel?
lessons.qsub: Tests pattern composition for a real-world, extensible system. Interviewers ask about adding new channels, prioritization, and failure handling.

lessons.name: "Design a document editor with undo/redo" (Command + Memento)
lessons.desc: Design text operations as Command objects. Each command stores state for undo (Memento). Command history stack enables undo/redo navigation.
lessons.q: Design a document editor with full undo/redo capability. How do you handle large document memory for undo history?
lessons.qsub: Classic problem that naturally fits Command + Memento composition. Tests understanding of undo semantics and state management.

lessons.name: "Design a cache with eviction policies" (Strategy + Proxy)
lessons.desc: Design a cache with pluggable eviction algorithms. Strategy (LRU, LFU, FIFO), Proxy (wrap data source), Singleton (cache manager).
lessons.q: Design a thread-safe cache with pluggable eviction policies. How would you implement LRU efficiently?
lessons.qsub: Cache design is a system design staple. Tests Strategy pattern in a performance-critical context with concurrency considerations.

lessons.name: "Design a workflow engine" (Chain of Resp + Command + State)
lessons.desc: Design a system that executes a series of steps with branching, parallel execution, and state persistence.
lessons.q: Design a workflow engine that supports sequential steps, branching, parallel execution, and state persistence.
lessons.qsub: Complex business process modeling. Tests how patterns compose across concerns: execution flow, state, and operation logging.

lessons.name: "Design a plugin system" (Strategy + Factory + Proxy)
lessons.desc: Architecture for loading third-party extensions at runtime. Strategy (plugin interface), Factory (discovery/instantiation), Proxy (sandboxed wrapper).
lessons.q: Design a plugin system that loads third-party extensions at runtime with security isolation.
lessons.qsub: Extensibility architecture is a senior engineer concern. Tests class loading, isolation, and contract design.

lessons.name: "Design a UI component library" (Composite + Decorator + Strategy)
lessons.desc: Design a reusable component system. Composite (component tree), Decorator (add styling/behavior), Strategy (rendering for themes).
lessons.q: Design a UI component library that supports theming and composable component trees.
lessons.qsub: Reflects real frontend architecture. Tests how patterns compose in a tree-based UI system. Example: React/Vue component architecture.

lessons.name: Strategy vs State — same structure, different intent (algorithm vs state machine)
lessons.desc: Strategy vs State — both have identical class structures (Context + interface + concrete classes). Difference is intent: Strategy selects algorithm, State manages behavior transitions.
lessons.q: Strategy and State have identical UML. How do you distinguish them by intent and usage?
lessons.qsub: Interviewers love this comparison. Both behavioral patterns with the same structure but different intent. Mixing them up is a common mistake.

lessons.name: Decorator vs Proxy — both wrap, but intent differs (add features vs control access)
lessons.desc: Decorator vs Proxy — both wrap an object and forward calls. Intent differs: Decorator adds new behavior, Proxy controls access.
lessons.q: How is the intent different between Decorator and Proxy when they both wrap objects? Give examples.
lessons.qsub: Distinguishing these shows depth. Both are structural wrappers but serve fundamentally different purposes.

lessons.name: Factory vs Builder — Factory creates in one step, Builder in multiple steps
lessons.desc: Factory vs Builder — Factory creates in one step (single method call). Builder creates in multiple steps, allowing different configurations.
lessons.q: When would you choose Builder over Factory? What problem does each solve?
lessons.qsub: Both are creational but suit different complexity levels. Builder handles complex objects with optional parts; Factory handles type selection.

lessons.name: Observer vs Mediator — Observer is distributed, Mediator is centralized
lessons.desc: Observer vs Mediator — both handle communication. Observer distributes (one-to-many notification). Mediator centralizes (many-to-many through coordinator).
lessons.q: When does Observer's distributed communication become a problem, and how does Mediator solve it?
lessons.qsub: Understanding the distinction reveals when to decouple directly (Observer) vs through a coordinator (Mediator).

lessons.name: Adapter vs Facade — Adapter changes interface, Facade simplifies
lessons.desc: Adapter vs Facade — both wrap something existing. Adapter converts one interface to another (interface transformation). Facade provides simplified interface (simplification).
lessons.q: What is the key difference in motivation between Adapter and Facade? Compare their level of abstraction.
lessons.qsub: Both are structural wrappers with different motivations. Adapter is for compatibility, Facade is for simplicity.

lessons.name: Command vs Strategy — Command has undo/redo, Strategy is interchangeable algorithms
lessons.desc: Command vs Strategy — both encapsulate behavior in objects. Command represents a request (action + parameters) with undo support. Strategy represents interchangeable algorithms.
lessons.q: How does Command's undo/redo capability distinguish it from Strategy which also encapsulates behavior?
lessons.qsub: Both behavioral, both encapsulate behavior. Command: what to do (with history). Strategy: how to do it (with swapping).

lessons.name: Null Object Pattern
lessons.desc: A Null Object implements the interface with no-op behavior. Client code works with real and null objects identically — no null checks needed. Common in UI trees (no-op component), logging (null logger), and caching (null cache that just doesn't cache).
lessons.q: How does the Null Object pattern eliminate null checks and where is it commonly used?
lessons.qsub: Eliminates null checks scattered throughout code — cleaner than optional/nullable handling everywhere.

lessons.name: Specification Pattern
lessons.desc: Specification pattern encapsulates business rules as composable objects. Each specification tests an object against a rule. Compose with AND, OR, NOT to build complex queries. Separates business logic from data access.
lessons.q: How does the Specification pattern encapsulate and compose business rules? How does it fit with the Repository pattern?
lessons.qsub: Business rules become first-class citizens that can be combined, tested, and reused — instead of scattered if-statements.
